blocks.en: Counseling Situations · Unit 3 · The Abused
blocks.es_reference: Situaciones de Consejería · Unidad 3 · El Abusado

blocks.en: The Abused
blocks.es_reference: El Abusado

blocks.en: "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). The abused need, first of all, to be believed, to be made safe, and to be told the truth: this was not their fault.
blocks.es_reference: "Cercano está Jehová a los quebrantados de corazón; y salva a los contritos de espíritu" (Salmo 34:18). El abusado necesita, antes que nada, ser creído, ser puesto a salvo, y que se le diga la verdad: esto no fue su culpa.

blocks.en: The Situation
blocks.es_reference: La Situación

blocks.en: Sooner or later someone will disclose to a pastor that they have been abused — a wife harmed by her husband, a child or teenager harmed by an adult, an adult carrying the wounds of abuse suffered long ago. The disclosure may come in a flood of tears or in a flat, halting voice; it may be the first time the person has ever told anyone. What the pastor does in that moment matters enormously, because the abused often carry not only the original wound but a crushing weight of shame, self-blame, and fear of not being believed — and a wrong response can deepen all three. So the pastor must settle several truths in his own heart before he ever sits with such a person. Abuse is always the fault of the abuser, never of the victim — no behavior, no failure, no provocation makes a person responsible for the wrong done to them. The abused are to be believed and taken seriously, not interrogated as suspects. And this is an area where a pastor, however loving, is not equipped to act alone: abuse involves real danger, often crime, and almost always the need for trained professionals and the proper authorities. The pastor's calling here is not to investigate, not to mediate between victim and abuser, and not to handle it quietly within the church, but to believe, to protect, to point to the God who is near the brokenhearted, and to bring in the help the situation requires.
blocks.es_reference: Tarde o temprano alguien le revelará a un pastor que ha sido abusado — una esposa dañada por su esposo, un niño o adolescente dañado por un adulto, un adulto que carga las heridas de un abuso sufrido hace mucho. La revelación puede venir en un torrente de lágrimas o en una voz plana y entrecortada; puede ser la primera vez que la persona se lo cuenta a alguien. Lo que el pastor hace en ese momento importa enormemente, porque el abusado a menudo carga no solo la herida original sino un peso aplastante de vergüenza, autoculpa, y miedo de no ser creído — y una respuesta equivocada puede ahondar los tres. Así que el pastor debe asentar varias verdades en su propio corazón antes de sentarse con tal persona. El abuso es siempre culpa del abusador, nunca de la víctima — ninguna conducta, ningún fallo, ninguna provocación hace a una persona responsable del mal que se le hizo. Al abusado se le debe creer y tomar en serio, no interrogar como a un sospechoso. Y esta es un área donde un pastor, por amoroso que sea, no está equipado para actuar solo: el abuso implica peligro real, a menudo delito, y casi siempre la necesidad de profesionales capacitados y de las autoridades apropiadas. El llamado del pastor aquí no es investigar, ni mediar entre víctima y abusador, ni manejarlo en silencio dentro de la iglesia, sino creer, proteger, señalar al Dios que está cerca de los quebrantados, y traer la ayuda que la situación requiere.

blocks.en: ⚠ Non-negotiable safeguards for this situation. These are not optional pastoral preferences; they protect life. (1) Believe and never blame. The victim is never responsible for the abuse, and the pastor never asks questions implying they are. (2) Safety first. If anyone is in present danger, getting them to safety comes before everything else. (3) Report. The abuse of a child or vulnerable person must be reported to the proper civil authorities; the pastor does not investigate it himself or keep it inside the church. (4) Never counsel the victim and the abuser together, and never pressure a victim toward "reconciliation" or "forgiveness" that returns them to danger. (5) Keep no secret that protects an abuser; a promise of secrecy must never be given. (6) Bring in trained professionals and the authorities — the pastor works alongside them, never in place of them.
blocks.es_reference: ⚠ Salvaguardas no negociables para esta situación. Estas no son preferencias pastorales opcionales; protegen la vida. (1) Crea y nunca culpe. La víctima nunca es responsable del abuso, y el pastor nunca hace preguntas que insinúen que lo es. (2) La seguridad primero. Si alguien está en peligro presente, llevarlo a un lugar seguro va antes que todo. (3) Reporte. El abuso de un niño o persona vulnerable debe reportarse a las autoridades civiles apropiadas; el pastor no lo investiga él mismo ni lo guarda dentro de la iglesia. (4) Nunca aconseje juntos a la víctima y al abusador, y nunca presione a una víctima hacia una "reconciliación" o "perdón" que la devuelva al peligro. (5) No guarde ningún secreto que proteja a un abusador; nunca debe darse una promesa de secreto. (6) Traiga profesionales capacitados y a las autoridades — el pastor trabaja junto a ellos, nunca en lugar de ellos.

blocks.en: Scripture does not look away from abuse. In 2 Samuel 13 it tells, in unflinching detail, the story of Tamar, a daughter of King David, raped by her half-brother Amnon. The text does not hide it, does not soften it, and does not for one moment suggest it was her fault — it names Amnon's act as the wicked, violent thing it was, and records Tamar's anguish with tender seriousness: she was, the text says, a "desolate woman." What is striking, and grievous, is what the people around her failed to do. Her brother Absalom told her to "be quiet now... do not take this to heart," silencing her; and her father David, though angry, did nothing to bring justice or to care rightly for his daughter. The silence and inaction of those who should have protected her compounded the wound. The Bible records this not to instruct us to imitate Absalom and David, but as a sober warning of what not to do — and the abused person before you has often already lived this story: harmed, then silenced, then failed by those who should have helped. The pastor is called to break that pattern: to refuse to silence, to refuse to look away, to believe, and to act for the protection and dignity of the one who was wronged.
blocks.es_reference: La Escritura no aparta la mirada del abuso. En 2 Samuel 13 cuenta, en detalle inflexible, la historia de Tamar, una hija del rey David, violada por su medio hermano Amnón. El texto no lo oculta, no lo suaviza, y no sugiere ni por un momento que fuera culpa de ella — nombra el acto de Amnón como la cosa malvada y violenta que fue, y registra la angustia de Tamar con tierna seriedad: ella quedó, dice el texto, "desconsolada." Lo que es impactante, y doloroso, es lo que las personas a su alrededor dejaron de hacer. Su hermano Absalón le dijo que "callara ahora... no se angustiara por esto," silenciándola; y su padre David, aunque se enojó, no hizo nada para traer justicia ni para cuidar rectamente a su hija. El silencio y la inacción de quienes debieron protegerla agravaron la herida. La Biblia registra esto no para instruirnos a imitar a Absalón y David, sino como una advertencia seria de lo que no se debe hacer — y la persona abusada ante usted a menudo ya ha vivido esta historia: dañada, luego silenciada, luego fallada por quienes debieron ayudar. El pastor es llamado a romper ese patrón: a negarse a silenciar, a negarse a apartar la mirada, a creer, y a actuar por la protección y la dignidad del que fue agraviado.

blocks.en: The Ten Steps, Applied to the Abused
blocks.es_reference: Los Diez Pasos, Aplicados al Abusado

blocks.en: Step One · Stage 1
blocks.es_reference: Paso Uno · Etapa 1

blocks.en: Determine the Time and the Place — Safety and Privacy
blocks.es_reference: Determinar el Tiempo y el Lugar — Seguridad y Privacidad

blocks.en: For the abused, the setting must above all be safe and unhurried. The person needs to know they will not be overheard, interrupted, or exposed, and that the abuser cannot walk in. The pastor honors the standing safeguard — never counseling someone of the opposite gender alone behind a closed door, but with a door open or a trusted, appropriate person present — and he weighs carefully who that person should be, ensuring it is someone safe for the victim and never anyone connected to the abuser. He gives unhurried time, because disclosures of abuse cannot be rushed; the person may need many minutes simply to feel safe enough to begin, and may tell only a fragment at first. And if the person is in present danger, the immediate question is not counseling at all but getting them to safety. The very first gift the pastor gives is a place where it is safe to speak.
blocks.es_reference: Para el abusado, el entorno debe ser sobre todo seguro y sin prisa. La persona necesita saber que no será escuchada por otros, interrumpida, ni expuesta, y que el abusador no puede entrar. El pastor honra la salvaguarda permanente — nunca aconsejando a solas a alguien del sexo opuesto tras una puerta cerrada, sino con una puerta abierta o una persona apropiada y de confianza presente — y sopesa con cuidado quién debe ser esa persona, asegurándose de que sea alguien seguro para la víctima y nunca alguien conectado con el abusador. Da tiempo sin prisa, porque las revelaciones de abuso no se pueden apresurar; la persona puede necesitar muchos minutos solo para sentirse lo bastante segura para empezar, y puede contar solo un fragmento al principio. Y si la persona está en peligro presente, la pregunta inmediata no es la consejería en absoluto sino llevarla a un lugar seguro. El primer regalo que el pastor da es un lugar donde es seguro hablar.

blocks.en: Step Two · Stage 1
blocks.es_reference: Paso Dos · Etapa 1

blocks.en: Listen — Believe, and Do Not Interrogate
blocks.es_reference: Escuchar — Crea, y no Interrogue

blocks.en: This is the heart of the first response, and it must be done right. The pastor listens with belief and compassion, letting the person tell as much or as little as they are able, at their own pace, without pressing for details they are not ready to give. He does not interrogate, does not play detective, does not ask "are you sure?" or "what did you do to cause this?" — questions that retraumatize and that wrongly shift blame onto the victim. He receives what is said as true and serious. Crucially, he never promises secrecy; if a person begins, "I'll tell you, but you have to promise not to tell anyone," the pastor gently does not make that promise, explaining with care that because he wants them safe, there may be people who need to help. (Gathering the detailed facts is the work of trained investigators and authorities, not the pastor — his listening is pastoral care, not investigation.) Above all, the abused person needs to hear, and to feel, that they have finally been believed.
blocks.es_reference: Este es el corazón de la primera respuesta, y debe hacerse bien. El pastor escucha con fe y compasión, dejando que la persona cuente tanto o tan poco como sea capaz, a su propio ritmo, sin presionar por detalles que no está lista para dar. No interroga, no juega al detective, no pregunta "¿estás seguro?" o "¿qué hiciste para causar esto?" — preguntas que retraumatizan y que equivocadamente trasladan la culpa a la víctima. Recibe lo que se dice como verdadero y serio. De modo crucial, nunca promete secreto; si una persona empieza, "te lo diré, pero tienes que prometer no decírselo a nadie," el pastor con suavidad no hace esa promesa, explicando con cuidado que porque los quiere a salvo, puede haber personas que necesiten ayudar. (Reunir los hechos detallados es el trabajo de investigadores capacitados y de las autoridades, no del pastor — su escucha es cuidado pastoral, no investigación.) Sobre todo, la persona abusada necesita oír, y sentir, que al fin ha sido creída.

blocks.en: Step Three · Stage 1
blocks.es_reference: Paso Tres · Etapa 1

blocks.en: Clarify the Situation — Safety and the Truth About Blame
blocks.es_reference: Aclarar la Situación — la Seguridad y la Verdad sobre la Culpa

blocks.en: Clarifying here has two urgent priorities, and neither is the gathering of evidence. The first is safety: Is the person in present danger? Is a child still in contact with the abuser? Is there a threat of further harm? Where there is present danger or a child or vulnerable person is involved, this moves immediately toward protection and the proper authorities. The second is the truth about blame: the pastor gently but clearly names what the abused person most needs to hear and so rarely believes — this was not your fault. Victims almost always carry false guilt, replaying what they might have done differently, and the pastor lovingly and repeatedly places the responsibility where it belongs: wholly on the one who chose to do harm. He clarifies, too, what abuse is, for some have been so conditioned that they do not recognize what was done to them as wrong. The goal of this step is not a detailed account of the events but two clear truths established: you are not to blame, and we will get you safe.
blocks.es_reference: Aclarar aquí tiene dos prioridades urgentes, y ninguna es la recolección de evidencia. La primera es la seguridad: ¿Está la persona en peligro presente? ¿Está un niño aún en contacto con el abusador? ¿Hay amenaza de más daño? Donde hay peligro presente o está involucrado un niño o persona vulnerable, esto se mueve de inmediato hacia la protección y las autoridades apropiadas. La segunda es la verdad sobre la culpa: el pastor con suavidad pero con claridad nombra lo que la persona abusada más necesita oír y tan rara vez cree — esto no fue tu culpa. Las víctimas casi siempre cargan una culpa falsa, repasando lo que podrían haber hecho distinto, y el pastor con amor y repetidamente coloca la responsabilidad donde pertenece: enteramente sobre quien eligió hacer el daño. Aclara, también, qué es el abuso, pues algunos han sido tan condicionados que no reconocen lo que se les hizo como malo. La meta de este paso no es un relato detallado de los hechos sino dos verdades claras establecidas: no eres culpable, y te llevaremos a un lugar seguro.

blocks.en: Step Four · Stage 1
blocks.es_reference: Paso Cuatro · Etapa 1

blocks.en: Investigate Previous Counseling — and the Need for Professionals
blocks.es_reference: Investigar la Consejería Previa — y la Necesidad de Profesionales

blocks.en: The pastor learns what help is already in place and what is urgently needed. Has the person told anyone before, and how were they received? Are they already working with a counselor, a doctor, an advocate, the authorities? Is there a safe support network around them? This step is, more than in any other situation, the recognition that the pastor must not work alone. Abuse calls for trained trauma professionals, for medical care where there is injury, for advocates who know the protective resources, and — where a child or vulnerable person has been harmed — for the civil authorities, who must be notified. The pastor's role is to be the faithful spiritual shepherd within a team of qualified helpers, not a substitute for them. To attempt to handle abuse alone, inside the church, is not only beyond his competence; it can endanger the victim and let harm continue. Knowing what help exists, and bringing in what does not yet, is itself a central act of care.
blocks.es_reference: El pastor conoce qué ayuda ya está en su lugar y qué se necesita urgentemente. ¿Le ha contado la persona a alguien antes, y cómo fue recibida? ¿Está ya trabajando con un consejero, un médico, un defensor, las autoridades? ¿Hay una red de apoyo segura a su alrededor? Este paso es, más que en cualquier otra situación, el reconocimiento de que el pastor no debe trabajar solo. El abuso pide profesionales capacitados en trauma, cuidado médico donde hay lesión, defensores que conozcan los recursos de protección, y — donde un niño o persona vulnerable ha sido dañado — las autoridades civiles, que deben ser notificadas. El papel del pastor es ser el pastor espiritual fiel dentro de un equipo de ayudantes calificados, no un sustituto de ellos. Intentar manejar el abuso solo, dentro de la iglesia, no solo está más allá de su competencia; puede poner en peligro a la víctima y dejar que el daño continúe. Conocer qué ayuda existe, y traer la que aún no, es en sí un acto central de cuidado.

blocks.en: Step Five · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Cinco · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Responsibility — Belongs to the Abuser, Never the Victim
blocks.es_reference: Responsabilidad — Pertenece al Abusador, Nunca a la Víctima

blocks.en: In every other situation in this course, Step Five gently helps a person own their part. Here that pattern is deliberately broken, and the break must be absolute: the victim bears no responsibility whatsoever for the abuse. Responsibility lies entirely and only with the abuser, who alone chose to do harm. The pastor must never, by any word or implied question, suggest the victim caused, invited, or deserved what was done — not by their dress, their behavior, their failures, their staying, or anything else. This is the single most important thing to get right in this unit, because the abused person almost always already blames themselves, and a careless word can drive that false guilt deeper. So the pastor actively and repeatedly works to lift the false guilt the victim carries, naming clearly that the shame they feel belongs to the one who harmed them, not to them. The only "responsibility" rightly placed on the victim is the gentle, supported invitation to take the steps toward their own safety and healing — and even that is offered as care, never as a demand, and never as anything they failed to do before.
blocks.es_reference: En cada otra situación de este curso, el Paso Cinco con suavidad ayuda a una persona a asumir su parte. Aquí ese patrón se rompe deliberadamente, y la ruptura debe ser absoluta: la víctima no carga ninguna responsabilidad en absoluto por el abuso. La responsabilidad recae entera y únicamente sobre el abusador, que solo él eligió hacer el daño. El pastor nunca debe, por ninguna palabra o pregunta implícita, sugerir que la víctima causó, invitó, o mereció lo que se le hizo — ni por su ropa, su conducta, sus fallos, su haberse quedado, ni nada más. Esto es lo más importante de acertar en esta unidad, porque la persona abusada casi siempre ya se culpa a sí misma, y una palabra descuidada puede ahondar esa culpa falsa. Así que el pastor activa y repetidamente trabaja para levantar la culpa falsa que la víctima carga, nombrando con claridad que la vergüenza que siente pertenece a quien la dañó, no a ella. La única "responsabilidad" rectamente puesta sobre la víctima es la suave y apoyada invitación a dar los pasos hacia su propia seguridad y sanación — y aun eso se ofrece como cuidado, nunca como exigencia, y nunca como algo que dejó de hacer antes.

blocks.en: Step Six · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Seis · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Model the Role
blocks.es_reference: Modelar el Papel

blocks.en: The pastor models, by his own steady response, the safety and respect the abused person may have long been denied. He stays calm and does not react with shock, disgust, or anger that the victim might mistake as aimed at them. He is gentle, patient, and entirely trustworthy — keeping his word, respecting the person's pace, never pushing past their consent in conversation. In doing so he becomes, often, a corrective experience: a relationship with an authority figure or a person of trust that is safe, honoring, and without exploitation, perhaps the first the person has known in a long time. He also models, quietly, the character of God toward the wounded — not the harsh or absent figures who failed them, but One who is near to the brokenhearted, who does not despise them, and who is angered by what was done to them. The way the pastor conducts himself preaches, before any words, that this person is worthy of respect and safety.
blocks.es_reference: El pastor modela, por su propia respuesta firme, la seguridad y el respeto que a la persona abusada quizá se le negaron por mucho tiempo. Se mantiene en calma y no reacciona con conmoción, asco, o ira que la víctima podría malinterpretar como dirigida a ella. Es gentil, paciente, y enteramente confiable — cumpliendo su palabra, respetando el ritmo de la persona, nunca empujando más allá de su consentimiento en la conversación. Al hacerlo se vuelve, a menudo, una experiencia correctiva: una relación con una figura de autoridad o una persona de confianza que es segura, honrosa, y sin explotación, quizá la primera que la persona ha conocido en mucho tiempo. También modela, en silencio, el carácter de Dios hacia el herido — no las figuras duras o ausentes que le fallaron, sino Uno que está cerca de los quebrantados de corazón, que no los desprecia, y que se enoja por lo que se les hizo. La manera en que el pastor se conduce predica, antes de cualquier palabra, que esta persona es digna de respeto y seguridad.

blocks.en: Step Seven · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Siete · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Review the Alternatives — Toward Safety and Healing
blocks.es_reference: Repasar las Alternativas — Hacia la Seguridad y la Sanación

blocks.en: The pastor helps the person see the real paths toward safety and healing — without ever pressuring a particular choice, since restoring a victim's sense of agency is itself part of healing. These paths include: getting to physical safety where there is danger, with the help of those who know how (advocates, shelters, authorities); the involvement of the proper authorities, especially where a child or vulnerable person has been harmed, which is not optional; professional trauma counseling, which the pastor warmly encourages; medical care where needed; and a safe, supportive community around the person. The pastor presents these as avenues of help and hope, walking the person through what each involves, and supports them in taking the steps — while recognizing that an adult victim makes their own decisions, and that pushing too hard can re-enact the control they have already suffered. The one place this yielding does not apply is the protection of a child or vulnerable person, which the law and conscience require regardless. The aim is a path out of danger and toward healing, taken with support and as much of the person's own choice as safety allows.
blocks.es_reference: El pastor ayuda a la persona a ver los caminos reales hacia la seguridad y la sanación — sin jamás presionar una elección particular, ya que restaurar el sentido de agencia de la víctima es en sí parte de la sanación. Estos caminos incluyen: llegar a la seguridad física donde hay peligro, con la ayuda de quienes saben cómo (defensores, refugios, autoridades); la participación de las autoridades apropiadas, especialmente donde un niño o persona vulnerable ha sido dañado, lo cual no es opcional; consejería profesional de trauma, que el pastor anima cálidamente; cuidado médico donde se necesite; y una comunidad segura y de apoyo alrededor de la persona. El pastor presenta estos como vías de ayuda y esperanza, acompañando a la persona por lo que cada uno implica, y la apoya en dar los pasos — reconociendo a la vez que una víctima adulta toma sus propias decisiones, y que presionar demasiado puede repetir el control que ya ha sufrido. El único lugar donde esta cesión no aplica es la protección de un niño o persona vulnerable, que la ley y la conciencia exigen sin importar nada. El objetivo es un camino fuera del peligro y hacia la sanación, tomado con apoyo y con tanta de la propia elección de la persona como la seguridad permita.

blocks.en: Step Eight · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Ocho · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Explore the Outcomes
blocks.es_reference: Explorar los Resultados

blocks.en: The pastor holds out honest hope: that with safety, support, professional help, and time, healing from even deep abuse is genuinely possible, and that the wound, though it has marked them, does not have to define or rule the rest of their life. He does not minimize — he never says "just get over it" or implies that healing will be quick or simple, for trauma runs deep and recovery is often long and not a straight line. But he refuses the lie abuse tells, that the person is permanently ruined or worthless. He helps them see that the path of safety and support, hard as it is, leads toward a real future — toward a restored sense of self, of dignity, of trust, and of the possibility of joy again — while the path of silence, isolation, and remaining in danger only prolongs the harm. And for the deepest wound abuse inflicts, the lie that one is dirty, worthless, or beyond love, he holds out the truth that no abuse can change a person's worth in the eyes of God, who calls them His own and treasures them.
blocks.es_reference: El pastor sostiene una esperanza honesta: que con seguridad, apoyo, ayuda profesional, y tiempo, la sanación de un abuso aun profundo es genuinamente posible, y que la herida, aunque los ha marcado, no tiene que definir ni gobernar el resto de su vida. No minimiza — nunca dice "solo supéralo" ni insinúa que la sanación será rápida o simple, pues el trauma corre hondo y la recuperación es a menudo larga y no una línea recta. Pero rechaza la mentira que dice el abuso, de que la persona está permanentemente arruinada o sin valor. Le ayuda a ver que el camino de la seguridad y el apoyo, por difícil que sea, lleva hacia un futuro real — hacia un sentido restaurado de sí mismo, de dignidad, de confianza, y de la posibilidad del gozo de nuevo — mientras que el camino del silencio, el aislamiento, y permanecer en peligro solo prolonga el daño. Y para la herida más honda que el abuso inflige, la mentira de que uno está sucio, sin valor, o más allá del amor, sostiene la verdad de que ningún abuso puede cambiar el valor de una persona a los ojos de Dios, que la llama suya y la atesora.

blocks.en: Step Nine · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Nueve · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Supply Information — God Is Near the Brokenhearted
blocks.es_reference: Proveer Información — Dios Está Cerca de los Quebrantados

blocks.en: When the person is ready — and the timing must follow their readiness, never be forced — the pastor brings the truths of Scripture that meet the deep wounds of abuse, gently and never as a demand. To the shame and sense of worthlessness, he brings the truth that God is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Psalm 34:18), that the person is fearfully and wonderfully made and precious in His sight, and that nothing done to them can make them dirty or unloved before God. To the feeling of being abandoned, he brings the God who sees the afflicted — like Hagar, who named Him "the God who sees me" — and who does not look away. He assures them that God is not indifferent to what was done: He is a God of justice who hates the violence done to the vulnerable and will set all things right. Two cautions guide him here. He does not press forgiveness of the abuser; that is a long, deep work that belongs to the victim and to God in time, never to be demanded, and never to be confused with reconciliation or with a return to danger. And he does not offer Scripture as a shortcut around the hard, slow work of healing, but as the deep ground of hope beneath it — the assurance that they are held by a God who is near, who sees, who loves them still, and who is angered on their behalf.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando la persona está lista — y el momento debe seguir su disposición, nunca ser forzado — el pastor trae las verdades de la Escritura que alcanzan las heridas hondas del abuso, con suavidad y nunca como una exigencia. A la vergüenza y al sentido de no valer nada, trae la verdad de que Dios está cerca de los quebrantados de corazón y salva a los contritos de espíritu (Salmo 34:18), de que la persona es formidable y maravillosamente hecha y preciosa a Su vista, y de que nada hecho a ellos puede hacerlos sucios o no amados ante Dios. Al sentimiento de estar abandonado, trae al Dios que ve al afligido — como Agar, que lo llamó "el Dios que me ve" — y que no aparta la mirada. Les asegura que Dios no es indiferente a lo que se hizo: es un Dios de justicia que aborrece la violencia hecha al vulnerable y enderezará todas las cosas. Dos advertencias lo guían aquí. No presiona el perdón del abusador; esa es una obra larga y honda que pertenece a la víctima y a Dios con el tiempo, nunca para exigirse, y nunca para confundirse con la reconciliación o con un regreso al peligro. Y no ofrece la Escritura como un atajo alrededor del trabajo duro y lento de la sanación, sino como el suelo hondo de esperanza debajo de ella — la seguridad de que son sostenidos por un Dios que está cerca, que ve, que los ama todavía, y que se enoja a favor de ellos.

blocks.en: Step Ten · Stage 2
blocks.es_reference: Paso Diez · Etapa 2

blocks.en: Provide Closure
blocks.es_reference: Proveer Cierre

blocks.en: Healing from abuse is long work, so closure is never a single conversation but a sustained, faithful walking-alongside — with the pastor as one steady part of a larger team of help. He makes sure the concrete protective steps are actually in place, not merely discussed: that safety is secured, the proper authorities involved where required, the professional help connected. He follows up, staying present through a recovery that will have hard days and setbacks, so the person is not abandoned once the crisis passes — the very abandonment Tamar suffered. He keeps the person surrounded by safe, supportive community, while guarding them from any pressure to "move on," to reconcile, or to keep the peace at the cost of their safety. And he keeps pointing them, gently and over time, to the God who is near the brokenhearted — not with quick answers, but with the steady, patient presence that itself testifies that they have not been left alone, and that they are worthy of being cared for all the way through.
blocks.es_reference: La sanación del abuso es obra larga, así que el cierre nunca es una sola conversación sino un sostenido y fiel caminar al lado — con el pastor como una parte firme de un equipo mayor de ayuda. Se asegura de que los pasos protectores concretos de veras estén en su lugar, no solo discutidos: que la seguridad esté asegurada, las autoridades apropiadas involucradas donde se requiera, la ayuda profesional conectada. Da seguimiento, permaneciendo presente a través de una recuperación que tendrá días difíciles y retrocesos, para que la persona no sea abandonada una vez que pase la crisis — el abandono mismo que Tamar sufrió. Mantiene a la persona rodeada de una comunidad segura y de apoyo, mientras la guarda de cualquier presión a "seguir adelante," a reconciliarse, o a mantener la paz a costa de su seguridad. Y sigue señalándola, con suavidad y a lo largo del tiempo, al Dios que está cerca de los quebrantados de corazón — no con respuestas rápidas, sino con la presencia firme y paciente que en sí testifica que no ha sido dejada sola, y que es digna de ser cuidada hasta el final.

blocks.en: Theory Lens — the Psychoanalytic Insight, Used With Care
blocks.es_reference: Perspectiva — la Idea Psicoanalítica, Usada con Cuidado

blocks.en: The Psychoanalytic tradition (rooted in Freud and those who followed) contributes one insight especially relevant to abuse: that deep wounds, particularly those suffered early or kept hidden, do not simply disappear when they are out of mind. They leave a lasting imprint, shaping a person's sense of self, their relationships, and their reactions in ways they may not consciously connect to the original harm. Buried pain has a way of surfacing — in anxiety, depression, difficulty trusting, shame, or patterns that repeat — and genuine healing usually requires that the hidden wound be brought, safely and with skilled help, into the light rather than left to fester in silence. This is real and useful wisdom for understanding the abused: it explains why "just forgetting it" does not work, why the effects can persist for years, and why professional trauma care matters. It also rhymes with a biblical instinct — that what is hidden in darkness needs to be brought into the light to be healed, and that God desires "truth in the inward being."
blocks.es_reference: La tradición Psicoanalítica (arraigada en Freud y quienes le siguieron) aporta una idea especialmente relevante al abuso: que las heridas hondas, en particular las sufridas temprano o mantenidas ocultas, no simplemente desaparecen cuando están fuera de la mente. Dejan una huella duradera, moldeando el sentido de sí mismo de una persona, sus relaciones, y sus reacciones de maneras que quizá no conecten conscientemente con el daño original. El dolor enterrado tiene una manera de salir a la superficie — en ansiedad, depresión, dificultad para confiar, vergüenza, o patrones que se repiten — y la sanación genuina por lo general requiere que la herida oculta sea traída, con seguridad y con ayuda capacitada, a la luz en lugar de dejarla enconarse en silencio. Esta es sabiduría real y útil para entender al abusado: explica por qué "solo olvidarlo" no funciona, por qué los efectos pueden persistir por años, y por qué el cuidado profesional de trauma importa. También hace eco de un instinto bíblico — que lo que está oculto en la oscuridad necesita ser traído a la luz para ser sanado, y que Dios desea "la verdad en lo íntimo."

blocks.en: The biblical caution. Yet the pastor must use this insight carefully and within firm limits. First, a matter of competence: understanding that buried trauma surfaces is not the same as being trained to treat it. Probing for buried memories, attempting depth work, or trying to excavate a person's past is the skilled and sometimes risky work of trained trauma professionals — done badly it can retraumatize or even generate false memories — and it is precisely not something the pastor should attempt. His role is to recognize that such wounds are real and lasting, and therefore to refer, not to dig. Second, a matter of truth: the psychoanalytic frame can drift toward treating the person mainly as the sum of their past determining their present, but the gospel insists they are more than what was done to them — a person made in God's image, of unchangeable worth, and capable, by grace, of real healing and a genuinely new future. And it can speak of guilt and shame only as feelings to be managed, where the gospel can do what no therapy can: lift the false shame that never belonged to the victim, and assure them they are clean, beloved, and held. So the pastor takes the genuine insight — hidden wounds need light and skilled care — and sets it within the larger truth that the abused person is precious to God, not defined by their wound, and bound for healing. The insight informs his understanding; it does not become his toolkit. For the work itself, he refers.
blocks.es_reference: La advertencia bíblica. Sin embargo el pastor debe usar esta idea con cuidado y dentro de límites firmes. Primero, una cuestión de competencia: entender que el trauma enterrado sale a la superficie no es lo mismo que estar entrenado para tratarlo. Sondear en busca de recuerdos enterrados, intentar trabajo profundo, o tratar de excavar el pasado de una persona es el trabajo capacitado y a veces arriesgado de profesionales de trauma entrenados — hecho mal puede retraumatizar o incluso generar recuerdos falsos — y es precisamente no algo que el pastor deba intentar. Su papel es reconocer que tales heridas son reales y duraderas, y por lo tanto referir, no excavar. Segundo, una cuestión de verdad: el marco psicoanalítico puede inclinarse a tratar a la persona principalmente como la suma de su pasado determinando su presente, pero el evangelio insiste en que son más que lo que se les hizo — una persona hecha a imagen de Dios, de valor inmutable, y capaz, por gracia, de una sanación real y un futuro genuinamente nuevo. Y puede hablar de la culpa y la vergüenza solo como sentimientos a manejar, donde el evangelio puede hacer lo que ninguna terapia puede: levantar la vergüenza falsa que nunca perteneció a la víctima, y asegurarle que es limpia, amada, y sostenida. Así que el pastor toma la idea genuina — las heridas ocultas necesitan luz y cuidado capacitado — y la coloca dentro de la verdad mayor de que la persona abusada es preciosa para Dios, no definida por su herida, y destinada a la sanación. La idea informa su entendimiento; no se vuelve su caja de herramientas. Para el trabajo mismo, refiere.

mc.stem: The single most important truth the pastor must establish with an abused person is:
options: That they must forgive their abuser immediately
That they must keep it confidential
That they should have left sooner
That the abuse was not their fault — responsibility lies wholly with the abuser

mc.stem: When a person says 'I'll tell you, but promise not to tell anyone,' the pastor should:
options: Promise secrecy to gain their trust
Refuse to listen at all
Gently decline to promise secrecy, explaining that because he wants them safe, others may need to help
Promise, then break the promise later

mc.stem: Regarding the abuse of a child or vulnerable person, the unit states the pastor must:
options: Investigate it himself and handle it within the church
Report it to the proper civil authorities; he does not investigate it himself or keep it inside the church
Keep it secret to protect the church's reputation
Wait until he is certain before telling anyone

mc.stem: In listening (Step Two), the pastor should NOT:
options: Interrogate, play detective, or ask questions like 'are you sure?' or 'what did you do to cause this?'
Believe the person and take them seriously
Let the person tell as much or as little as they are able
Receive what is said as true and serious

mc.stem: Why is Step Five (Responsibility) deliberately handled differently in this unit?
options: Because the victim shares some of the blame
Because responsibility does not matter here
Because the victim bears no responsibility whatsoever; it lies entirely with the abuser, and the pastor works to lift the victim's false guilt
Because the pastor should assign blame carefully

mc.stem: Regarding the victim and the abuser, the unit says the pastor must never:
options: Counsel them together, or pressure the victim toward reconciliation or forgiveness that returns them to danger
Believe the victim
Involve the authorities
Offer the victim hope

mc.stem: In the account of Tamar (2 Samuel 13), the unit highlights that:
options: Scripture blames Tamar for what happened
Scripture names the abuse plainly, does not blame the victim, and shows the failure of those who silenced her as a warning
Tamar should have stayed quiet
The story has nothing to teach pastors

mc.stem: Regarding forgiveness of the abuser (Step Nine), the pastor should:
options: Demand it quickly as proof of faith
Make it a condition of further help
Tell the victim the abuse was minor
Not press it; it is a long, deep work belonging to the victim and God in time, never demanded, never confused with reconciliation or a return to danger

mc.stem: The genuine insight the Psychoanalytic tradition offers for understanding abuse is that:
options: Victims should simply forget what happened
Deep, hidden wounds leave a lasting imprint and resurface, so healing usually requires bringing them safely into the light with skilled help
The past has no effect on the present
The pastor should excavate buried memories himself

mc.stem: The biblical caution on the psychoanalytic insight includes that the pastor should:
options: Recognize such wounds are real and refer to trained professionals — not dig himself — and hold that the person is more than their past, precious to God
Probe for buried memories and attempt depth work himself
Treat the person only as the sum of their past
Manage guilt and shame as mere feelings

fill.prompt: "The LORD is near to the ____ and saves the crushed in spirit" (Psalm 34:18).
Abuse is always the fault of the ____, never of the victim.
The pastor keeps no secret that protects an abuser; a ____ of secrecy must never be given.
The abuse of a child or vulnerable person must be ____ to the proper civil authorities.
In 2 Samuel 13 Scripture tells the story of ____, a daughter of King David, raped by her half-brother Amnon.
After Tamar was wronged, her brother ____ told her to be quiet, silencing her.
Victims almost always carry ____ guilt, replaying what they might have done differently.
The pastor does not press a particular choice, since restoring a victim's sense of ____ is itself part of healing.
To the feeling of being abandoned, the pastor brings the God who sees the afflicted, like ____, who named Him "the God who sees me."
Since buried wounds are real and lasting, the pastor's role is to ____, not to dig.

sa.prompt: List the non-negotiable safeguards a pastor must hold when ministering to someone who has been abused.
sa.model: These safeguards protect life and are not optional. (1) Believe and never blame: the victim is never responsible for the abuse, and the pastor never asks questions implying they are. (2) Safety first: if anyone is in present danger, getting them to safety comes before everything else. (3) Report: the abuse of a child or vulnerable person must be reported to the proper civil authorities; the pastor does not investigate it himself or keep it inside the church. (4) Never counsel the victim and the abuser together, and never pressure a victim toward reconciliation or forgiveness that returns them to danger. (5) Keep no secret that protects an abuser; a promise of secrecy must never be given. (6) Bring in trained professionals and the authorities, working alongside them rather than in place of them. The pastor's calling is to believe, protect, point to the God who is near the brokenhearted, and bring in the help the situation requires.

sa.prompt: Why must the pastor never promise secrecy, and how should he listen when someone discloses abuse?
sa.model: The pastor must never promise secrecy because a promise of silence can protect an abuser and leave someone in danger; if a person says 'promise not to tell anyone,' he gently declines, explaining with care that because he wants them safe, there may be people who need to help. As he listens, he listens with belief and compassion, letting the person tell as much or as little as they are able, at their own pace, without pressing for details. He does not interrogate, play detective, or ask 'are you sure?' or 'what did you do to cause this?' — questions that retraumatize and wrongly shift blame onto the victim. He receives what is said as true and serious. Gathering the detailed facts is the work of trained investigators and authorities, not the pastor; his listening is pastoral care, not investigation. Above all, the abused person needs to hear and feel that they have finally been believed.

sa.prompt: Explain why Step Five (Responsibility) is handled differently here than in every other unit, and what the pastor actively does instead.
sa.model: In every other situation, Step Five gently helps a person own their part. Here that pattern is deliberately and absolutely broken: the victim bears no responsibility whatsoever for the abuse. Responsibility lies entirely and only with the abuser, who alone chose to do harm. The pastor must never, by any word or implied question, suggest the victim caused, invited, or deserved what was done — not by their dress, behavior, failures, staying, or anything else. This is the most important thing to get right, because the abused person almost always already blames themselves, and a careless word can drive that false guilt deeper. So instead of helping them 'own their part,' the pastor actively and repeatedly works to lift the false guilt the victim carries, naming clearly that the shame they feel belongs to the one who harmed them, not to them. The only 'responsibility' rightly placed on the victim is the gentle, supported invitation to take steps toward their own safety and healing — offered as care, never as a demand, and never as something they failed to do before.

sa.prompt: How does the account of Tamar (2 Samuel 13) instruct the pastor in how to respond — and how not to?
sa.model: Scripture does not look away from abuse: in 2 Samuel 13 it tells in unflinching detail the rape of Tamar by her half-brother Amnon. The text does not hide or soften it, and never suggests it was her fault — it names Amnon's act as wicked and violent, and records Tamar's anguish with tender seriousness, calling her a desolate woman. What is grievous is the failure of those around her: her brother Absalom silenced her ('be quiet now... do not take this to heart'), and her father David, though angry, did nothing for justice or for her care. Their silence and inaction compounded the wound. The Bible records this not so we imitate Absalom and David but as a sober warning of what not to do. The abused person before the pastor has often already lived this story — harmed, then silenced, then failed by those who should have helped. The pastor is called to break that pattern: to refuse to silence, refuse to look away, believe, and act for the protection and dignity of the one who was wronged.

sa.prompt: What genuine insight does the Psychoanalytic tradition offer about abuse, and what two cautions (competence and truth) must guide the pastor in using it?
sa.model: The psychoanalytic insight is that deep wounds, especially those suffered early or kept hidden, do not simply disappear; they leave a lasting imprint and resurface — in anxiety, depression, difficulty trusting, shame, or repeating patterns — so genuine healing usually requires bringing the hidden wound safely into the light with skilled help rather than leaving it to fester. This explains why 'just forgetting it' fails and why professional trauma care matters, and it rhymes with the biblical instinct that what is hidden needs light. Two cautions guide its use. Competence: understanding that buried trauma surfaces is not the same as being trained to treat it; probing for buried memories or attempting depth work is skilled, sometimes risky professional work that can retraumatize or create false memories, so the pastor recognizes the wound is real and refers rather than digs. Truth: the psychoanalytic frame can drift toward treating a person as merely the sum of their past, but the gospel insists they are more than what was done to them — made in God's image, of unchangeable worth, capable by grace of real healing. And where it can only manage guilt and shame as feelings, the gospel lifts the false shame that never belonged to the victim and assures them they are clean, beloved, and held. The insight informs the pastor's understanding; it does not become his toolkit. For the work itself, he refers.

sa.prompt: What truths must the pastor settle in his own heart before he ever sits with an abused person, and what is his calling in that situation?
sa.model: Abuse is always the fault of the abuser, never of the victim; no behavior, failure, or provocation makes a person responsible for the wrong done to them. The abused are to be believed and taken seriously, not interrogated as suspects. And this is an area where a pastor is not equipped to act alone, since abuse involves real danger, often crime, and the need for trained professionals and the proper authorities. His calling is not to investigate, not to mediate between victim and abuser, and not to handle it quietly within the church, but to believe, to protect, to point to the God who is near the brokenhearted, and to bring in the help the situation requires.

sa.prompt: What are the two urgent priorities of 'Clarify the Situation' with an abused person, and what is this step not about?
sa.model: The first priority is safety: whether the person is in present danger, whether a child is still in contact with the abuser, whether there is a threat of further harm; where there is present danger or a child or vulnerable person is involved, this moves at once toward protection and the proper authorities. The second is the truth about blame: the pastor gently and clearly names what the person most needs to hear and rarely believes, this was not your fault, placing the responsibility wholly on the one who chose to do harm, and he clarifies what abuse is for those so conditioned they do not recognize it as wrong. The step is not the gathering of evidence or a detailed account; its goal is two clear truths, you are not to blame and we will get you safe.

sa.prompt: Why does the pastor 'model the role' differently with the abused, and what does his conduct communicate about God?
sa.model: He stays calm and does not react with shock, disgust, or anger the victim might mistake as aimed at them; he is gentle, patient, and entirely trustworthy, keeping his word, respecting the person's pace, never pushing past their consent. In this he becomes a corrective experience: a relationship with a person of trust or authority that is safe, honoring, and without exploitation, perhaps the first in a long time. He also quietly models the character of God toward the wounded, not the harsh or absent figures who failed them but One who is near the brokenhearted, does not despise them, and is angered by what was done to them; his conduct preaches that this person is worthy of respect and safety.

sa.prompt: How does the pastor review the alternatives with an adult victim, and where does the principle of letting the person choose not apply?
sa.model: He lays out the real paths toward safety and healing without pressuring a particular choice, since restoring the victim's sense of agency is itself part of healing: physical safety with the help of advocates, shelters, and authorities; professional trauma counseling; medical care where needed; and a safe, supportive community. He walks through what each involves and supports the steps, recognizing that an adult makes their own decisions and that pushing too hard re-enacts the control they have already suffered. The one place this yielding does not apply is the protection of a child or vulnerable person, which the law and conscience require regardless.

sa.prompt: Which Scriptures does the pastor bring to the wounds of abuse, and what two cautions govern how he brings them?
sa.model: When the person is ready, never forced, he brings Psalm 34:18, God is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit; that the person is fearfully and wonderfully made and precious in His sight, and nothing done to them can make them dirty or unloved; the God who sees the afflicted, as Hagar named Him; and the God of justice who hates violence against the vulnerable and will set all things right. Two cautions: he does not press forgiveness of the abuser, a long work belonging to the victim and God, never demanded and never confused with reconciliation or a return to danger; and he does not offer Scripture as a shortcut around the slow work of healing, but as the deep ground of hope beneath it.
